newsitem.title: USA: Clinton a captive of U.S. activism in Mideast.
newsitem.headline: Clinton a captive of U.S. activism in Mideast.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's high-stakes effort to revive the Middle East peace process continues a tradition of U.S. presidential involvement in the byzantine world of Arab-Israeli politics that started with Harry Truman.

With just five weeks left before his political fate is to be decided in a November 5 election clash with Republican Bob Dole, Clinton clearly would have preferred to avoid the messy foreign policy distraction that has the potential to damage his so-far smooth-running bid for a second term.

But U.S. officials said it was not an option for Clinton to stand by and watch escalating violence between Israel and the Palestinians, because that could mean risking the unravelling of years of painstaking presidential diplomacy.

"The United States has often played a pivotal role in bringing Arabs and Israelis together to work out their differences in peace," Clinton said in summoning Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to Washington.

"It is our responsibility to do whatever we can to protect the peace process and to help move it forward. This is such a moment," Clinton said. Jordan's King Hussein will also take part in the talks, and Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa will be a consultant.

Truman, a Democrat who served in the White House from 1945 to 1953, started the process of U.S. engagement in the Middle East when he overruled his advisers and extended U.S. recognition to Israel within hours of its proclamation of statehood in 1948.

His action was driven partly by politics -- American Jews were, and are, a key Democratic Party constituency; partly by moral considerations -- Americans were repulsed and outraged by the Nazi genocide of the Jews in the Second World War; and partly by personal loyalty to an old friend.

The friend was Eddie Jacobson, Truman's onetime partner in a Kansas City, Missouri, men's clothing store. In his memoirs, Truman said a visit from Jacobson persuaded him to commit U.S. prestige and influence in the Middle East.

"In all my years in Washington, he (Jacobson) had never asked me for anything for himself. He was of the Jewish faith and was deeply moved by the suffering of the Jewish people abroad," Truman said in his memoir, "Years of Trial and Hope".

U.S. engagement was relatively low-key from a foreign policy standpoint until Israel's rout of Egypt, Syria and Jordan in the 1967 Six-Day War. That turned the Middle East into a Cold War powder-keg as Washington and Moscow tried to outflank each other in the region.

The intense superpower rivalry triggered a U.S. nuclear alert during another Arab-Israeli conflict six years later -- the 1973 Yom Kippur War -- and the beginnings of the Middle East peace process that now seems in danger of collapse.

Republican Presidents Richard Nixon and Gerald Ford pioneered shuttle diplomacy, sending Secretaries of State William Rogers and Henry Kissinger to the region to coax Israel and the Arabs into a halting first step toward peace -- a disengagement of forces in Egypt's Sinai desert.
Their initiatives and a stunning 1977 visit to Israel by Egyptian President Anwar Sadat, who was later assassinated, helped Democrat Jimmy Carter engineer the Camp David accords.

Carter himself shuttled between Israel and Egypt in 1979 to translate the Camp David breakthrough into a peace treaty between Israel and Egypt, but follow-on Arab-Israeli agreements proved elusive until Clinton took office in 1993.

Reaping some of what was sown by Republican George Bush, who ended the old Cold War rivalry in the Middle East and created a new dynamic for peace in the region with the U.S.-led Gulf War victory over Iraq, Clinton presided over two agreements: limited self-rule for the Palestinians in 1993 and a peace agreement between Israel and Jordan in 1994.

He hoped to crown his first term with a peace pact between Israel and Syria, but the assassination of Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, a wave of terrorist bombings in Tel Aviv and Jerusalem and the election of hardliner Netanyahu as Israeli prime minister derailed that effort.

Now Clinton is fighting to save what has already been achieved, and his aides are trying to keep expectations low. White House spokesman Mike McCurry says the summit will be a success if Netanyahu and Arafat agree "to do everything within their power to end the violence ... (and) show a renewed commitment to address their differences in the negotiations."
